extracted.intended_audience: judges, appellate lawyers, and legal scholars focused on administrative and environmental law (especially EPA regulation and statutory interpretation)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-analysis guidance for assessing the scope of EPA's authority under Clean Air Act §111(d), including how to read statutory text, history, precedent, and agency expertise when evaluating rules like the Clean Power Plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 111(d) purpose as a 'gap-filler' / backstop
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) guarantees that 'there should be no gaps in control activities pertaining to stationary source emissions that pose any significant danger to public health or welfare.' (S. Rep. No. 91–1196, p. 20 (1970)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat §111(d) as a backstop ensuring pollutants not regulated through other programs (NAAQS, HAP) are nonetheless regulated; it operates to ensure comprehensive pollution control and so should be read to fill regulatory gaps rather than as an 'ancillary' or 'backwater' provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory mandate for the 'best system' and emission limit (§7411(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the [EPA] Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.' §7411(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting standards, EPA must identify a 'best system of emission reduction' that has been 'adequately demonstrated,' consider costs, nonair impacts, and energy requirements, and set the particular emissions limit 'achievable' through applying that system. These statutory components are meaningful constraints on agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider costs, nonair impacts, and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision tells EPA, in making that determination, to take account of both costs and varied 'nonair' impacts (on health, the environment, and the supply of energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and agencies must treat the statutory instructions to consider cost and nonair impacts as operative constraints that shape what measures may qualify as the 'best system.' Prior rulemakings excluded some measures for failure to satisfy these considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that the 'best system' be 'adequately demonstrated' (proven track record)
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision instructs EPA to decide upon the 'best system of emission reduction which . . . has been adequately demonstrated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'adequately demonstrated' requirement demands empirical or evidentiary support; EPA should exclude measures lacking a proven track record of effectiveness or demonstration in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'system' broadly — includes coordinated sets of measures (e.g., cap-and-trade, generation shifting)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA stated the 'plain meaning' of 'system' in §111 refers to 'a set of measures that work together to reduce emissions.' Dictionaries define 'system' as 'a complex unity formed of many often diverse parts subject to a common plan or serving a common purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read 'system' comprehensively rather than narrowly as solely equipment-level technological fixes; statutory usage and dictionary definitions support inclusion of market mechanisms like cap-and-trade and generation-shifting approaches as lawful 'systems' of emission reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use related statutory provisions and internal statutory usage to interpret terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Other Clean Air Act provisions describe cap-and-trade as an 'emission allocation and transfer system' (§7651(b)) and allow trading as 'control measures, means, or techniques' (§7410(a)(2)(A)); §7411(d)(1) directs EPA to use a procedure 'similar to that provided by [the NAAQS].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference the Act's other provisions and its own usage of terms to determine meaning; consistent usage across the statute supports interpreting §111 to permit mechanisms like trading/generation-shifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to congressional omission of textual limits (legislative history and amendment choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress in 1977 struck 'technological' from the standard for existing sources (contrasting the 'best technological system' for new sources), and later deleted the technological limitation for new facilities in 1990.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Congress includes a limitation in some provisions but omits it in others, that choice is informative: the absence of a 'technological' qualifier in §111 for existing sources signals congressional intent to allow non-technological measures; courts should respect such legislative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess fit between agency action and the broader statutory design (conflict/misfit test)
rubrics_metrics.description: In prior cases the Court rejected agency actions that 'simply did not fit' the statutory scheme because the action conflicted with or would 'wreak havoc on' Congress's broader design (e.g., Brown & Williamson, Utility Air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether allowing the agency's construction would render other statutory provisions meaningless, require rewriting express statutory terms or numeric thresholds, or otherwise upset the statute's structure; such misfit suggests Congress did not authorize the claimed power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether the agency is operating within its traditional lane or comparative expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have been skeptical where agencies have attempted to decide issues outside their expertise or traditional domain (e.g., FDA regulating tobacco, Attorney General regulating medical judgments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the agency's expertise relative to the subject matter; when a policy decision implicates domains outside the agency's practical competence, courts should question whether Congress intended to delegate that authority to the agency. Conversely, EPA has recognized expertise here (e.g., regulating powerplant emissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine — extraordinary cases require clear congressional authorization (as applied by majority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority describes a 'major questions doctrine' requiring, in 'certain extraordinary cases,' that the agency 'must point to clear congressional authorization for the power it claims' beyond the normal statutory basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents an interpretive trigger that raises the bar for agency authority in high‑magnitude disputes; the dissent criticizes it as a departure from ordinary text-in-context interpretation. Either way, identify whether a case is 'extraordinary' and whether additional, clear congressional authorization exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do ordinary text-in-context and 'common sense' delegation analysis first
rubrics_metrics.description: The words of a statute 'must be read in their context and with a view to their place in the overall statutory scheme' and courts 'must be guided to a degree by common sense as to the manner in which Congress is likely to delegate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply normal tools of statutory construction — textual reading, context, and purposive/common-sense assessment of congressional delegation — before invoking any heightened presumptions; examine how Congress typically delegates similar matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'broad' statutory language from 'vague' language
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad term is comprehensive, extensive, wide-ranging; a 'vague' term is unclear, ambiguous, hazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate breadth with vagueness; use dictionary definitions, statutory context, and surrounding constraints to determine whether a broad term supplies sufficient guidance for agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the practical magnitude and real-world effect of the regulation rather than assume 'transformative' consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'bigness' or 'transformative' label is not dispositive; empirical evidence about actual market behavior and regulatory impact matters (the Clean Power Plan apparently would have had little or no net effect because industry behavior already met its goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess record evidence about the regulation's real-world effects (e.g., market responses, industry compliance) to determine whether the rule truly has the sweeping consequences claimed; an asserted large-scale effect absent supporting empirical showings is less persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical administrative practice and recognized regulatory tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Generation shifting and cap-and-trade have a well-established pedigree; state regulators and power companies have long used such techniques to attain environmental goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that longstanding or common administrative tools (market-based mechanisms, generation shifting) are within the agency's toolbox and bolster claims that such measures fit within statutory delegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress speaks plainly when circumscribing authority and in capacious terms when enlarging it
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Congress knows to speak in plain terms when it wishes to circumscribe, and in capacious terms when it wishes to enlarge, agency discretion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive presumption: when statutory text is capacious, courts should be reluctant to insert judicial limits absent clear textual indicators; conversely, clear textual limits should be given effect where Congress so expressed itself.
